When I have the chance, I try to leave home five minutes earlier than usual and stop by a bar near my bus stop for a coffee. The newspapers on the counter still smell fresh, and the employees juggle the tasks of serving early risers while cleaning and preparing the establishment for the new day. It's a centrally located bar, well-positioned in a busy area, with lunch menus and slot machines buzzing all day.

At this hour, the early birds mix with the night owls. The baker and the police officer share the space, coffee with milk next to a final drink before bed. I stir the sugar in my coffee and take in my surroundings, appreciating what I see. The tireless housewife, now with grown children, dedicates herself to housework in other homes: tired but content. The smell of deodorant and freshly applied cologne, the starch in ironed shirts. The atmosphere is one of a new day, of unwrapping fresh starts, of hardworking laborers.

People greet each other warmly and sincerely, with the camaraderie of early risers who share a common goal: to start the day with energy, with the hope that everything will go well today. It feels like a very exclusive private club, a community united by the basics. I'm glad to be part of this group, looking around, greeting, and smiling with my eyes.

I remember being a child and occasionally accompanying my father for his first coffee of the morning. I recall how he would enter the bar and confidently say, "Good morning," and people would respond. It always impressed me.

Being naturally shy and introspective, my father's confident greetings always amazed me. He spoke with the assurance of someone who knew he would get a reply. Why wouldn't they? I looked at him and saw someone big, strong, and self-assured. He was the figure who could do anything, in whom I had complete trust, the one who held his hands out for me to rest my head and relax. Though I didn’t realize then how unsteady those hands might have been, I closed my eyes calmly because he was keeping watch that night and every night.

Time has passed, and now it's me who says good morning, expects a response, and receives it. I understand the role I'm stepping into and, most importantly, the role my father played then.

I admire the strict discipline he always showed in front of me. This image, among other things, shaped my emerging character. Now I understand that the confidence he radiated was an effort, a willpower, that no one truly walks through life with such determination. But I seem to have absorbed the message well and believe I apply it successfully in my life.

I leave some coins next to my coffee, pick up my hat from the counter, and give one last greeting to my fellow patrons. It was brief but intense. The looks exchanged carry hope, determination, and passion: now the new day really begins. As I leave the bar, people's expressions change; the personal moment ends, and thoughts turn to the day's work. It's not a bad expression, not sadness or resignation. It's focus, organizing tasks, diving into the workday.

Only one fleeting thought clouds my mood: I remember these bars being much fuller at this hour in the past. The thought passes quickly; I don't let it linger and dismiss it promptly. I pull my hat down a bit more, take a deep breath because it rained a little, and the asphalt has that distinctive, almost clean smell. I get on the bus and start writing.
